title: Pull your ears
hook: nodding Moggallana is given remedies for drowsiness: from pulling your ears to walking

segments.voice: Yesterday: Suppavasa's meal, and your line, a gift that comes back. Who did you feed? Today, what happens after a good meal, when you sit down to meditate and your head starts to drop. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

The breath is slow, the room is warm, and then your chin dips toward your chest, and you jerk back up, hoping no one saw. Anyone who has sat to meditate knows that moment. In the Book of Sevens, it happens to Moggallana, one of the Buddha's two chief disciples, famous in the tradition for his powers of mind. He's sitting in meditation near a village in Magadha, and he keeps nodding. The Buddha, the text says, sees it from far away, and comes to him with a list of remedies. Today: pacala.
screen: `THE CHIN DIPS.` → `EVEN MOGGALLANA NODDED.` → `A LIST OF REMEDIES.`

segments.voice: Are you nodding, Moggallana? the Buddha asks. Yes, sir. Then comes a ladder, each step tried only if the one before doesn't work. First: whatever thought you were on when drowsiness came, stop giving it attention. Second: if that fails, think over a teaching you've learned. Third: recite a teaching out loud, in detail. Fourth: pull both your earlobes and rub your limbs with your hands. Fifth: get up, wash your eyes with water, and look around in every direction, and up at the stars. Sixth: bring to mind the perception of light, the idea of daytime, day and night alike. Seventh: walk up and down, with your senses gathered in. And if none of that works? Eighth: lie down on your right side, like a lion, mindful, with the thought of getting up again, and when you wake, get up promptly. Notice how practical this is. No one is scolded. Sleepiness isn't treated as a sin, just as a state with causes and cures. Thinking, then talking, then the body, then cold water and open sky, then movement, and last of all, permission to rest. The order matters. Most of us skip straight to the last step, or fight the first one forever. And then the sutta keeps going, with advice on pride and on argument. But the ear-pulling is the part people remember.
screen: `ARE YOU NODDING, MOGGALLANA?` · `THINK, RECITE, PULL YOUR EARS.` · `WATER, STARS, LIGHT, WALKING.` · then, large: `LAST OF ALL, REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try one remedy. Sit up, and notice your level of alertness right now, honestly. If it's low, try the fourth step: gently take both earlobes between thumb and finger and give them a slow pull. Rub your hands together, then along your arms. Feel the body wake. If you're already alert, simply rest with the breath, and notice what alertness feels like, so you'll know it when it fades. The bell holds the time.

pacala. The Pali word for nodding or drowsiness, the state of Moggallana in the Book of Sevens, met by the Buddha with a ladder of remedies from changing the thought to looking at the stars. Today's word.
Your line: climb the ladder. Today, when the afternoon slump comes, climb the ladder: change the thought, splash water, look at the sky, walk. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions still give these remedies for sleepiness, such as opening the eyes, standing, or switching to walking meditation, and some retreats offer standing or walking periods for exactly this.

fork.setup: you're meditating and keep nodding off. you've tried thinking of a teaching and reciting one. what's the next remedy in the sutta?
options: pull your earlobes and rub your limbs.
fork.reveal: pull both earlobes and rub your limbs. after that come cold water and the stars, then walking, and last of all, rest.

original.note: Pali pacala: nodding, drowsiness; the sutta's name, 'the nodding discourse.'

trapdoor: what you thought: dozing off in meditation means you've failed.
what it means: the Buddha treats drowsiness as a state with causes and a ladder of cures.
what a scholar hears: the same sutta goes on to warn Moggallana against visiting families with 'trunk raised' in pride, and against quarrelsome talk.

notes: AN 7.58 paraphrased. Confirm the order of the eight remedies and the setting (Kallavalaputta in Magadha).
Confirm the Buddha 'sees from far away' by psychic power per the text; the script says only 'sees it from far away'.
Confirm Devanagari पचला and the stress mark; the sutta name may be given as Pacala or Capala in different editions.
Numbering of AN 7 suttas differs between editions (7.58 vs 7.61); confirm.
